verses.translation_literal: A song, a psalm, to the sons of Korah. To the choirmaster, upon Mahalath, for afflicting. A maskil, to Heman the Ezrahite.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song, a psalm, from the sons of Korah. For the choirmaster, to be sung to the tune called Mahalath, the melody of sickness and sorrow. A maskil, a poem of teaching, set in the name of Heman the Ezrahite.
verses.directors_commentary:
Read this line as a label on a scroll, not as a speech; the actor should say it flatly, because the oddest thing about it is how much of it nobody can fully decode. The KJV gives 'Mahalath Leannoth' as if it were a place or a tune name and moves on. The Hebrew words are probably a tune cue (the same word, Mahalath, heads Psalm 53), but they can also be read as 'sickness' and 'to afflict' or, from another root, 'to answer' or 'to raise the voice'. Rashi reads it as the sickness of love and the torment of exile, Ibn Ezra as the sickness of the poet, Metzudat Zion as a musical instrument and 'raising the voice'. That ambiguity is the doorway: before one word of the psalm is sung, the title already says 'sickness' to a Hebrew ear.

The title is verse 1 in the Hebrew, which is why the English verse numbers run one behind. Two names are attached: the sons of Korah, a guild of Levite singers, and Heman the Ezrahite, a sage. Whether Heman is the Levite singer of Chronicles or the Judahite sage of Solomon's court is disputed; Rashi, Radak and Meiri discuss both. Do not play him as a famous man; play him as a man whose name was attached to this one poem that has no sunrise in it.

philological_notes.note: A tune cue or a descriptive tag. 'Mahalath' may mean 'sickness' (root חלה), and 'le'annot' may be 'to afflict' (ענה II) or 'to sing/answer' (ענה I). Both fit; neither is certain.
From the root for insight; a poem meant to instruct or a skilful composition. It stands over a psalm that has no consolation, which is part of the irony.
'The Ezrahite', most likely 'of the clan of Zerah' (Judah), so a native-born sage; Ibn Ezra offers 'native' as another sense.

token_glosses.gloss: a maskil (a skilful or instructive poem)

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, God of my salvation, [by] day I have cried out, in the night before you.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, God of my salvation, I have cried out by day, and now, in the night, I stand before you still crying.
verses.directors_commentary:
The only warm phrase in the whole psalm is the opening: 'God of my salvation'. Speak it as a man reaching for a rail on a dark staircase. The KJV smooths the second half into the common phrase 'day and night'; the Hebrew is lopsided: 'day I cried out, in the night before you', with no 'and', and no verb in the second clause. The English softens an unfinished sentence. Ibn Ezra takes 'day' with the words that follow, which would leave the cry open-ended; Radak and Rashi hold that 'day' and 'night' name the same day-and-night span.

The night here is not decoration. For a sick or wretched man in an ancient house, night is when work stops, noise stops, and there is nothing left to distract from pain; Meiri notes that night is the time free of tasks, so it is the time of prayer. The actor should hold the final word 'before you' and not resolve it.

philological_notes.note: 'My salvation / rescue'. The root is the one behind the name Yeshua; the psalm begins with the language of rescue and then never receives it.
A cry of distress, the cry of one wronged or in danger, stronger than a calm 'call' (קרא), which the psalmist uses in verse 10.

verses.translation_literal: May my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my ringing cry.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my prayer come into your presence. Bend your ear down to my cry.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two imperatives, two pictures: a petition walking into a throne room, and a great figure leaning down to listen. 'Incline your ear' is physical; a king on a raised seat has to tip his head to hear a petitioner on the floor. Play it with open palms.

The KJV 'cry' is fine but flattens רִנָּה. Elsewhere it is a ringing shout, often of joy; here it is turned inside out, the same loud voice used for pain. Radak glosses it as a shout (cf. 'the cry passed through the camp'), which shows the word means volume, not mood. Ibn Ezra distinguishes the two lines: 'prayer' is the intention of the heart, 'cry' is what the tongue does.

philological_notes.note: A ringing or shrill cry. The word usually belongs to praise and gladness; here it is the only sound the speaker has left.

verses.translation_literal: For my being is sated with troubles, and my life has reached to Sheol.
verses.translation_dramatic: For my soul has had its fill of troubles, and my life has come down to the very edge of Sheol.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the psalm's first bitter joke. The verb שָׂבְעָה means 'to be full, to have eaten enough'; it is the word for a satisfied guest at a feast, and the Bible's good death is 'old and full of days' (the verb's cousin). Malbim catches it: the usual ideal is a man satisfied with goodness and years, but this man is satisfied with troubles. Say 'full' as a diner pushing back the plate.

The KJV 'draweth nigh unto the grave' makes this gentle and slow. The Hebrew verb הִגִּיעוּ is a perfect, 'have reached / touched', and the destination is שְׁאוֹל, Sheol, the underworld of the dead, not a grave in the ground (the KJV elsewhere translates the same word 'hell', 'pit' or 'grave' as the mood strikes). The BBE 'underworld' is closest. Nefesh is not 'soul' as in the later Western sense; it is the whole living self, throat, breath and appetite, which is why it can be 'sated'.

philological_notes.note: 'Is sated', the language of a full meal, turned on its head: the speaker has been fed troubles. Malbim contrasts the biblical blessing of dying 'full of days'.
The underworld, the shadowy place where all the dead gather. Not hell in the later sense. The KJV renders it 'the grave' here.

verses.translation_literal: I am reckoned with those who go down [to] the pit; I have become like a man [in whom] there is no strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: They count me already among those who go down into the pit. I have become a man with nothing left in him, no strength at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Reckoned' is bookkeeping language: someone has done the sum and entered him in the column of the dead. The sentence is passive, and nobody is named; the actor can leave it ambiguous whether it is neighbours, God, or the speaker's own tally. Malbim pictures a man in a faint whom the onlookers take for dead and are ready to bury while he still feels everything.

The 'pit' (בּוֹר) is the cistern-shaped hole in the rock that was used as a grave or a dungeon; to 'go down' is the usual verb for burial. אֱיָל is a rare word for strength; the KJV 'no strength' is right, while the ASV 'no help' follows a different guess. Rashi ties it to the similar word in Psalm 22:19, and Metzudat Zion to the strong rams of Ezekiel 31.

philological_notes.note: 'I have been reckoned', a passive of the verb for counting and accounting. The speaker is entered in the register of the dead.

A rare word for strength; Rashi compares Psalm 22:20 (Hebrew numbering), Metzudat Zion compares Ezekiel 31 where the related word names a strong one. Ibn Ezra reads it as a noun with an elided 'to him'.

verses.translation_literal: Among the dead, set free; like the slain who lie [in] a grave, whom you do not remember again, and they, from your hand, are cut off.
verses.translation_dramatic: Free, they call it, among the dead. Like the slain lying in their graves, the ones you remember no more, cut off from your hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse starts on a sour paradox: חָפְשִׁי is the word for a slave released from service. The KJV and Webster print 'Free among the dead' without any sign that it is bitter; the ASV's 'cast off' guesses at the meaning instead. In Israel's law a freed man walked out of his master's house with his obligations ended. The dead are 'free' in the same cold way: no work, no worship, no tax, no relationship. Ibn Ezra reads this as release from commandments and the labour of the body; Radak and Malbim read it as a wish ('would that I were among the dead'). The actor can take either: relief or horror, but the word should crack.

The second half is the harder blow. 'Whom you remember no more' means more than forgetting; in Hebrew, to remember is to act on someone's behalf (God 'remembered Noah'). Being un-remembered is being left outside the covenant's care. 'Cut off from your hand' means they no longer receive anything from God's hand, neither blessing nor blow. Malbim's reading is the cruellest: the dead are cut off from God's striking hand, but the speaker, still alive, is not.

philological_notes.note: 'Free', the word for a freed slave (Exodus 21). Among the dead it means released from every obligation, and also from every connection. The bitterness is in the contrast with freedom as a gift.
'You do not remember them'. Remembering in Hebrew is acting for someone, so to be unremembered is to be outside God's care.
'Cut off', as one cuts a branch or divides a thing. Metzudat Zion links it to Ezekiel 37:11, the dried bones that say 'we are cut off'.

verses.translation_literal: You have put me in a pit of the lowest parts, in dark places, in depths.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have set me in the pit of the lowest places, in the dark places, down in the depths.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speaker names who has done it: 'you', the one he called 'God of my salvation' five verses ago. In the Hebrew the word 'you' is built into the verb ('you have put me'), and the verb is set first. Play the shift from pleading to accusation as a drop in the voice, not a raised one.

Three nouns pile down, each deeper than the last: 'the pit of the lowest parts', 'dark places', 'depths'. The KJV's 'lowest pit' loses the plural; the Hebrew is lowest places, plural, a whole underworld cellar. מְצוֹלוֹת also means the deep of the sea, the place where Pharaoh's army sank like a stone; the word is spelled with an unusual vowel, which Meiri notes is a scribal oddity. Rashi and Radak read the whole line as a picture of exile; Ibn Ezra, as the sickbed.

philological_notes.note: 'In dark places', plural; the same root as 'darkness'. A Hebrew idiom for the underworld and for hiding places beneath the earth.
The depths of the sea, where things sink (Exodus 15:5, Nehemiah 9:11). Meiri observes the unusual vocalization with holem and lists both parallels.

verses.translation_literal: On me your wrath has leaned, and [with] all your breakers you have afflicted [me]. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your wrath has leaned its whole weight on me, and all your breakers have broken over me. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is a drowning man at the bottom of the sea with a weight pressed on top of him. סָמְכָה is the verb of leaning a hand or body on something, as a worshipper leans a hand on an offering; the wrath is not a flash but a sustained pressure. The KJV 'lieth hard upon me' is good. Meiri lists the alternatives (nearness, surrounding, strengthening) and the ancient doubt about the word.

מִשְׁבָּרִים are breakers, the waves that break on the shore, from the root 'to break'; the KJV 'waves' loses the smashing. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion all say so. 'Afflicted' (עִנִּיתָ) is the same root as the 'affliction' of the title. Selah is a marker we cannot place; take it as a beat of silence, an instrumental pause or a lifting of the voice, and let the room hang.

philological_notes.note: 'Your breakers', waves as they break (root 'to break'). Ibn Ezra links the verse to the image of the sea in the previous verse.
To lean on, rest one's weight on, support; here it is the wrath that leans. Meiri collects several senses (nearness, surrounding, strengthening).

verses.translation_literal: You have put my acquaintances far from me; you have made me abominations to them; shut in, and I cannot go out.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have driven my friends away from me. You have made me a horror to them. I am shut in, and I cannot get out.
verses.directors_commentary:
Isolation, in three steps: the friends are sent away, the man becomes repulsive to them, and he is locked in. All three verbs are God's doing in the speaker's grammar, which is why this is more accusation than complaint. The KJV 'mine acquaintance' sounds like a pleasantry; מְיֻדָּעַי are those 'known to me', the circle of people who know you by name, the people who would sit with you. Metzudat Zion pairs it with 'my companions and my familiar friends' of Psalm 55.

תּוֹעֵבוֹת is a plural of intensity, 'abominations', the strong word for what is ritually and socially revolting, used for idols and unclean food. The KJV 'an abomination' is correct in force; the Hebrew plural is closer to 'a thing of horrors'. The disease of a sufferer made him unclean in the eyes of neighbours; Ibn Ezra reads the 'shut in' as the confinement of illness, while Rashi reads it as imprisonment. A listener in the temple would hear both.

philological_notes.note: 'Those known to me', the circle of intimates. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'my loved ones' and compares Psalm 55.
Abominations; the plural makes the speaker a source of revulsion, not just an object of it.
'Shut up, confined'; the noun 'prison' (כֶּלֶא) is from the same root. Rashi reads it as imprisonment, Ibn Ezra as illness.

verses.translation_literal: My eye has wasted from affliction; I have called you, YHWH, every day; I have spread out to you my palms.
verses.translation_dramatic: My eye has wasted away with affliction. Every day I have called to you, O LORD, and every day I have spread my open hands out to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the accusation of the last verses comes the prayer posture. Stretching out the palms, open and upward, was the ancient gesture of petition, the empty hands of a beggar; Metzudat David says it is simply 'the way of those who pray'. The verb שִׁטַּחְתִּי is 'to spread flat', the verb for laying out nets or spreading cloth to dry. The actor's hands should be wide, not lifted in triumph.

The eye that 'wasted' is the eye dimmed by weeping or sickness; the sources split between tears (the Targum has the eye 'flowing with tears') and the sunken look of the ill (Ibn Ezra, Meiri). The KJV 'mourneth' is a poetic choice, not a literal one. Two words here play on the same sound: 'ani' (affliction) and 'eyni' (my eye). Note also the change of verb: where verse 2 had 'cried out' (צעק), here the psalmist has 'called' (קרא) in the calm voice of one who has tried every day.

philological_notes.note: 'Has pined, languished, grown faint'; of the eye, it dims and sinks with grief or illness. Metzudat Zion ties it to 'languishing of soul' in Deuteronomy 28.
'I have spread out my palms', the gesture of prayer. Metzudat David: 'as is the way of those who pray'.

verses.translation_literal: For the dead will you do a wonder? Or will the shades rise, will they give thanks to you? Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the dead, will you work a wonder? Will the shades rise up to thank you? Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speaker argues his case like a man in a law court, and the argument is a bargain: if you let me die, you lose a worshipper. This is not a creed about the afterlife; Radak is careful to say that the question concerns the nature of the world, not the later resurrection. The ancient Israelite view was that the dead are silent (Psalm 115:17), so praise belongs to the living. The question demands a 'no'. Play it with rising pitch and no answer.

The KJV makes the second line a plain repeat, 'shall the dead arise', and loses the new word. The Hebrew changes from מֵתִים, the dead, to רְפָאִים, the Rephaim, the shades or the weak ones of Sheol. Metzudat Zion derives the word from 'slackness' (רפיון), the limp, powerless dead. The word is spelled like 'healers' (רפא), and a Hebrew ear may hear the pun that the ones who are not healed rise not to heal. פֶּלֶא is the 'wonder' of the Exodus, the word God's saving acts carry; the question asks whether God does such deeds for those past saving.

philological_notes.note: A wonder, a marvel; the word used for God's mighty acts, especially the Exodus. The speaker asks whether a corpse can be the audience of one.
The shades of the dead in Sheol, 'the weak ones'. Metzudat Zion derives it from 'slackness'. The sound resembles רפא 'heal'; this link is my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: Will your covenant loyalty be recounted in the grave, your faithfulness in Abaddon?
verses.translation_dramatic: Can your loyal love be told in the grave? Can your faithfulness be told in the place of Destruction?
verses.directors_commentary:
The case rests on one idea: God's loyalty is something people tell. Praise, in ancient Israel, was storytelling, the repeating aloud of what God has done; a grave is the one place where no stories are told. The question sets the two great covenant words side by side: חֶסֶד, steadfast covenant love (the KJV 'lovingkindness' is a Coverdale coinage that has outlived its time), and אֱמוּנָה, faithfulness or reliability. The verb 'recount' (סָפַר) is the one for counting and telling in the same breath.

The second place name is אֲבַדּוֹן, 'Destruction', the name of the grave as the place where things perish. The KJV 'destruction' and the ASV's capitalised 'Destruction' show the translators felt it was a name; Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all gloss it as the grave. It is not yet the angel of Revelation 9. Meiri observes that the question does not deny resurrection but speaks of the order of nature. Malbim spells out the logic: wonders are done so that they can be known and told, and a corpse can neither know nor tell. The verse ends there, with no answer from God.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: faithful action within a bond. The KJV's 'lovingkindness' is a sentimental coinage; the sense is loyalty that holds.
'Destruction', a name for the place where the dead perish. Radak: 'the grave, where the body is lost and consumed'. Metzudat David agrees.

verses.translation_literal: Will it be known in the darkness, your wonder, and your righteousness in the land of forgetting?
verses.translation_dramatic: Will anyone know your wonders down in the dark? Will your justice be spoken of in the land where everything is forgotten?
verses.directors_commentary:
Two questions, and the answer to both is meant to be no. The speaker, a man who has been dying for a lifetime, argues from what the dead are thought to be: in Israel's picture of Sheol nobody praises, nobody remembers, nobody tells the story of what God has done. The 'wonders' are the saving acts the Psalms keep rehearsing; the 'righteousness' is God's faithful, covenant-keeping action, not mere fairness. If the singer dies, the stage loses a witness, and that is the pressure behind the plea. Play it as an argument, not as despair: he is bargaining.

The KJV's 'in the dark' is fair, but its 'forgetfulness' turns a place into an abstraction. The Hebrew says 'the land of forgetting', a country with a border, whose only product is oblivion; Radak glosses it as the grave where the dead are forgotten. The word נשיה occurs only here, and Metzudat Zion ties it to the root of 'God has made me forget' (Gen 41:51). The first line also has a small grammatical edge: 'wonder' is singular in form, collective in sense. BBE's 'where memory is dead' paraphrases well but loses 'land'.

philological_notes.note: 'Forgetting'. A hapax legomenon, the name of a place in which nothing is remembered; an abstract noun used as a geography. Related to the root in Manasseh's naming (Gen 41:51).
'Your righteousness' here is God's saving, faithful action toward his people, not abstract justice; the question is whether anyone in Sheol can recount it.

verses.translation_literal: And I, to you, YHWH, I have cried for help, and in the morning my prayer comes to meet you.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I, I have cried out to you, LORD. And every morning, before the day has taken shape, my prayer is already at your door.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first word is a hinge: 'And I', in sharp contrast with the dead of the last verse. The living still call. 'Cry for help' (שוע) is the loud, public cry of someone in need, not quiet devotion, and the pronoun comes first for emphasis, so the line pivots to the singer's persistent action. The morning is the traditional hour of divine rescue and of the first sacrifice, and also, as Ibn Ezra notes, the hour when the sick feel a little lighter.

The KJV 'shall my prayer prevent thee' is archaic: 'prevent' means 'go before' (Latin praevenire), and modern readers take it as 'stop'. The verb קדם means to meet, to confront, to come ahead of. Radak reads it as prayer coming before every other business of the day; Malbim pictures it as the first thing to arrive before God each morning. The KJV also reads the verb as a future, where YLT and BBE have present and past; the Hebrew imperfect is habitual: 'comes, keeps coming'. Note that the divine name stands in the middle of the line, so that the two halves frame it.

philological_notes.note: 'It comes to meet you / comes ahead of you'. The KJV 'prevent' keeps the older sense 'precede'; the verb is habitual, a daily arrival.
'I have cried for help': a loud, urgent cry to a rescuer, not a prayer in the abstract. Ibn Ezra stresses that the cry goes to God alone, not to a human physician.

verses.translation_literal: Why, YHWH, do you reject my soul? Do you hide your face from me?
verses.translation_dramatic: Why, LORD? Why do you cast my very self aside? Why do you hide your face, and turn it from me?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the question the whole psalm has been circling, and it comes out as a bare "Why?" The word לָמָה, "why", is a plea, not a request for information. The speaker does not ask for an explanation; they ask to be seen. Play it low and exhausted rather than angry, because the verse before has just told us that prayer has gone up every morning and nothing has come back.

The verb זָנַח is stronger than the KJV's "castest off". It is the word used elsewhere for a king discarding something worthless, and for God abandoning his people (Ps 44:10, 44:24). The object is נַפְשִׁי, which the KJV renders "my soul", but נֶפֶשׁ is the whole living self, the throat that breathes and swallows. So the speaker is saying "you throw me away", and the body is included. In the second half, "hide the face" is the standard Hebrew image for divine absence, and it turns on the priestly blessing: "YHWH make his face shine upon you" (Num 6:25) and "YHWH lift up his face to you" (Num 6:26). Every Israelite knew those words, so a hidden face here is the blessing run backwards. The KJV supplies "Lord" where the Hebrew has the name YHWH, which makes the address less intimate than it is.

A small point of syntax: the second clause has no "why" of its own. The first "why" carries both questions, which lets the two verbs press against each other without a breath between them.

philological_notes.note: "You reject" or "cast off". It is the verb of divine abandonment (Ps 44:10, 74:1), a stronger word than neutral "leave", and it implies the thing is judged unwanted. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as "abandon" (תעזוב).

"You hide your face" is the idiom for God withholding attention and favor. Radak reads it as God not turning toward the speaker's cry or prayer. It reverses the priestly blessing of Num 6:25-26, in which God's face shines and is lifted toward the people.

verses.translation_literal: Afflicted am I, and expiring from youth; I have borne your terrors; I am numbed.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am bowed down, and I have been dying for as long as I can remember. I have carried your terrors until there is nothing left in me to feel. I stand here stunned.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker steps back and looks at their whole life. עָנִי אֲנִי, "afflicted am I", puts the word first, so the poverty and suffering come before the person. Here the actor should not shout. This is a person stating the facts of a long illness, and the weariness is the drama.

The key phrase is וְגֹוֵעַ מִנֹּעַר, and it has two live readings. Most of the tradition takes מִנֹּעַר as "from youth": the speaker has been "expiring" or on the edge of death since boyhood. Radak and Meiri understand it so, as a life of suffering from the days of youth, and Metzudat David adds that there were few days of ease. The KJV follows this with "ready to die from my youth up", which is right in outline, though "ready to die" is a little mild; גָּוַע is the verb for actually breathing one's last, used of the flood dead (Gen 7:21). Rashi reads the word differently, as a sudden choking death, linking מִנֹּעַר to the verb for "shaking" (the Lord "shook off" the Egyptians in Exod 14:27). The consonants allow both, and a performer can let the second sense shadow the first.

Then comes אֵמֶיךָ, "your terrors". The KJV's "while I suffer thy terrors" smooths a plain perfect verb, "I have borne", into a present participle. And the last word, אָפֻנָה, occurs only here. The tradition splits: Rashi hears "fixed in place", terror settled in the heart; Radak and Meiri hear the word פֶּן, "lest", the constant dread that something worse will happen. The KJV's "distracted" and the BBE's "no strength" are guesses at the same edge. Play it as a numb, stunned freeze. The speaker has been afraid so long that fear has become a standing condition.

philological_notes.note: Most naturally "and expiring from youth": a continuing state of near death since youth. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read it that way. Rashi offers a different reading, a sudden, choking death, taking מנער from the root of "shaking" as in Exod 14:27, "YHWH shook off the Egyptians". Both are possible because the consonants are the same.
"Your terrors", from אֵימָה, dread. Metzudat Zion connects it with אימה and פחד, fear and dread. The suffix makes God the source of the terrors.

A word found only here. Rashi: "settled and fixed", from the word for "on its wheels, fitting" (אָפְנָיו, Prov 25:11). Radak and Meiri: from פֶּן, "lest", so "I fear continually that something will befall me". Metzudat Zion: "free, turned away" (פנוי). Whether it is a verb or a noun-like form is uncertain; the rendering "numbed" is a judgment.

verses.translation_literal: Over me have passed your angers; your terrors have utterly cut me off.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your anger has gone over me like a flood over a field. Your terrors have cut me down, and cut again, until nothing is left standing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The images turn violent. חֲרוֹנֶיךָ, "your anger", is plural in Hebrew, so the KJV's "thy fierce wrath" is a reasonable summary, but the Hebrew counts the angers one by one. The root חרה means to burn, and the speaker has been scorched. עָבְרוּ, "have passed", is the verb for water or a storm sweeping over (Ps 42:8, Ps 124:4), so the image is of being overrun rather than singled out. The KJV's present "goeth over" hides that these are completed events.

The last word is a rare and heavy form, צִמְּתוּתֻנִי, and it is built to be felt. The root צמת means to cut off or destroy; it is the verb used elsewhere for annihilation (Ps 94:23). The ending has an extra syllable, which the tradition reads in two ways. Radak and Meiri take the doubling as intensive: not one cutting but many, "cut me off again and again", in the manner of words like ירקרק, "very green". Ibn Ezra reads it as a compound form, like מַבְלִיגִיתִי in Jer 8:18, but Radak explicitly rejects that explanation. Whichever view holds, the sound is an echo that stutters, a speech so hit by blows that the word cannot finish cleanly. The KJV's "have cut me off" gives only the single stroke.

בִּעוּתֶיךָ, "your terrors", is a plural of intensity from בעת, "to terrify"; Metzudat Zion compares it with Isa 21:4. Note the pairing with the previous verse: אֵימֶיךָ, then בִּעוּתֶיךָ. The speaker has now named God's terrors twice, and both times God is the agent.

philological_notes.note: "They have cut me off", with an unusual extended ending. Radak and Meiri read the extra letters as intensive, meaning cut off many times over, like ירקרק. Ibn Ezra reads it as a compound form, like מבליגיתי; Radak says that explanation makes no sense. Metzudat Zion ties the root to "cutting off", as in Ps 94:23.
"Your terrors", a noun from the verb "to terrify", found only in the plural. Radak derives it from נִבְעַת, Metzudat Zion from בעתה, sudden panic.

verses.translation_literal: They have surrounded me like water all the day; they have encircled upon me together.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long they close around me like water, and together they ring me in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The anger and terror of the last verse become a besieging force. Two verbs of encircling, סבב and נקף, are stacked as a poet's double line; Radak says the doubling is simply Hebrew parallelism. Water here is not refreshing but rising: it surrounds, it rises, it leaves no side open. Malbim notes the second verb adds that they came all at once, not one after another. The 'all the day' marks that there is no relief: the morning prayer of verse 14 meets a day-long assault.

The KJV 'daily' for כל היום is a slight weakening; it is 'all the day', continuous, not once per day. And the KJV misses that the plural verbs have no stated subject: Metzudat David supplies 'the wrath and the terror' from verse 17, which I follow. Hebrew has a quiet pun in the sounds, סבוני … הקיפו, two hissing sequences like waves.

philological_notes.note: 'They have encircled': the besieger's verb; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as turning round.
'Together, at once': all the assailants at one time; the sense that there is no gap.

verses.translation_literal: You have put far from me lover and friend; my acquaintances, darkness.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have driven away everyone who loved me, every friend. My only companion now is the dark.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends with no answer, no turn to praise, and this is the point: it is the only individual lament that closes in darkness. The singer's last charge is that God himself has removed his friends. A sick person in the ancient Near East was contagious and ritually suspect, so friends and neighbours kept away, and the shame of it was part of the illness; God is named as the author because he is the author of everything.

The last line has no verb and sits in the ear like a door shutting: 'my acquaintances — darkness'. The KJV supplies 'into darkness' and so makes the friends disappear into it; ASV copies it. YLT reads 'my acquaintance is the place of darkness'. Rashi: 'I have become dark and cut off from them'. Radak and Meiri: 'as if my friends were in a dark place that I cannot see them'. The sound of the first word 'darkness' here (מחשך) also echoes the darkness of verse 13, so the psalm ends where its first argument began. Malbim, on the national reading, hears the whole people as a dying body.

philological_notes.note: 'My acquaintances, those known to me', literally 'my known ones'; a passive participle of the verb 'to know', echoing the 'will it be known' of verse 13.
'Darkness', a place of darkness; as a bare final word it can read as the predicate or the whole of the singer's company.
